title: Redwood structured output & function-calling demo - FinPay
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-22
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~54m
Attendees: Aaron Lin, Maya Chen - Redwood; Mark Rivera, Sana Patel, Jon Park - FinPay

Summary:
Redwood AE/SE ran a 45-50 minute structured output + function/tool-calling demo focused on JSON mode, schema validation, and guardrails. Customer is evaluating for payment fraud detection tooling and transaction enrichment pipelines. Key concerns: deterministic output, latency for high-QPS endpoints, VPC/on-prem options for PCI scope, and auditability (audit logs/KMS).

Topics:
- Structured output JSON mode (schemas, validation, error handling)
- Function/tool calling, e.g., enrichment webhooks and DB writes
- Guardrails and hallucination mitigation (schema enforcement, recaller/validation hooks)
- Deployment options: hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) and PCI considerations
- Performance and benchmarking (p99 latency, batching, caching)
- Next steps: security docs, pilot POC, pricing for dedicated capacity

Transcript:
[00:00] Aaron (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Aaron Lin, I'm the AE on the account. With me is Maya Chen, our Solutions Engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Mark (FinPay CTO): Good, thanks. We just grabbed coffee. Excited to see the structured output stuff you showed in the playbook.
[00:18] Maya (Redwood SE): Awesome. Today we'll walk through JSON mode, function-calling, and show how schemas and guardrails keep outputs deterministic. We'll also hit on deployment options since you mentioned PCI scope.
[00:28] Sana (Head of ML): Quick ask up front - we need very strict schema adherence. Our downstream processors expect fixed fields. If the model emits different shapes, it's a big ops headache.
[00:38] Maya: Totally understood. That's the core of the demo. We'll show automatic schema validation and a graceful failure path.
[00:45] Jon (Platform Eng): Also curious about latency when we enforce schema checks and do tool calls - is that inline or async?
[00:53] Aaron: Good callout. We'll describe both modes - sync function calls for synchronous enrichment, async webhook patterns for higher throughput. We'll also surface config for timeouts and retries.
[01:02] Maya: Okay jumping into the console. Sorry, my screen share is a little laggy, bear with me. (audio: slight click)
[01:18] Maya: Here is the Redwood Console. I'm going to run a structured output demo in JSON mode. The prompt is a payment transaction with a few attributes; we want the model to return a JSON object with fields: transaction_id, risk_score (0-100), reason_codes (list), merchant_category, enriched_data {customer_risk_flag, mcc_code}.
[01:40] Maya: First step: we bake a JSON schema into the request. You can see the schema panel. If the model returns anything non-compliant, Redwood can either auto-retry with a system prompt, run a sanitizer, or return an explicit error.
[01:55] Mark: When it retries, does it count as extra token usage for billing?
[02:00] Aaron: Yes, retries are billed as normal tokens. But there's config for keeping retries minimal - you can set max_retries and sample temperature to reduce non-determinism. Also caching for identical prefixes can save tokens.
[02:12] Sana: For our use case, failures must be observable and have audit logs - we need visibility into what failed and why.
[02:20] Maya: Absolutely. Console shows structured failure logs. Each failed response stores raw model output, schema diff, and the retry attempts. Those are available in the Console and via the API for ingestion into ELK / Splunk.
[02:35] Jon: And encryption for those logs? They need to be customer-managed keys.
[02:40] Aaron: Support for KMS/HSM and we've got an option to push audit logs to your VPC bucket in Private deployments.
[02:47] Maya: Back to the demo, I'll run a live function call. We're going to call an external enrichment tool - simulated here - to fetch merchant metadata. Watch the call payload and the function signature.
[03:05] Maya: (runs demo) The model returns a JSON object with a tool_call placeholder: {"tool": "merchant_enrich", "args": {"merchant_id": "m_123"}}. Redwood automatically maps that to a function call and hits the configured endpoint with a signed request.
[03:25] Mark: That signed request - is it proxied through Redwood or direct to our endpoint?
[03:30] Maya: Two options. Hosted API can proxy and sign on your behalf; Private/Dedicated can be configured to call your internal endpoint directly via VPC peering or private network. For PCI you probably want direct, internal-only connectivity.
[03:44] Sana: Do you support schema-level assertions on tool responses? For example, merchant_enrich must return mcc_code as 4-digit string.
[03:52] Maya: Yes. There are post-tool validators. If the tool returns invalid schema, Redwood can trigger a fallback: return error, call a secondary tool, or mark the transaction for human review.
[04:05] Jon: Any limitations on payload size or rate limits for tool calls? We do high QPS on lookups.
[04:12] Aaron: For Hosted, we have per-account rate limits; for Dedicated we can provision capacity and custom quotas to handle your QPS. Tool endpoints are rate-limited at the connector level but you can use batching where appropriate.
[04:25] (brief crosstalk)
[04:30] Maya: Now I'll flip to API mode to show the request/response. The API payload includes the schema, the function signature in JSON schema, and the preference for sync vs async.
[04:45] Maya: Example response: HTTP 200 with body containing a structured JSON with both the model output and metadata: token_counts, latency_ms, model_version, compliance_flags. This metadata helps correlate downstream processing.
[05:05] Mark: How deterministic is the risk_score? We need stable scores across versions, or at least a clear mapping when models are updated.
[05:13] Maya: You can pin model versions for production routes, and Redwood has rollout tools - canary, A/B, and auto-fallback. We also store per-request model_version and sampling parameters so you can re-run or compare. We recommend pinning in production and using a canary group for updates.
[05:30] Sana: For retraining signals, we need payloads that fail schema or low confidence. Can you surface confidence metrics?
[05:38] Maya: Yep, we expose model confidence proxies (like token-level probabilities) and a quality score from Redwood Optimize. We can attach these to your audit logs and create alerts when quality regresses against a prompt set.
[05:50] Mark: Let's talk latency. Our SLA target is p95 < 120ms for lookup-enriched responses. Is that realistic?
[05:58] Aaron: It depends on model size and batching. For small instruction-tuned models in quantized form on dedicated GPUs, sub-100ms token latency is possible for short outputs. But when you do inline tool calls that add network hops, the end-to-end will increase. For strict SLAs, Dedicated with local tool endpoints is best.
[06:18] Jon: If we go Dedicated, do you manage the infra or do we?
[06:22] Aaron: Redwood Dedicated is reserved capacity we operate for you; it's logically isolated and we provide monitoring and SRE support per SLA. For Private on-prem, you manage the infra but we provide the control plane and installers.
[06:34] Sana: Can we do an air-gapped on-prem deployment? PCI sometimes requires that.
[06:38] Maya: Yes, we have an on-prem package for air-gapped environments. There are extra steps for model onboarding and kernel compatibility, but it's supported.
[06:48] Mark: Walk me through an example failure flow again - if schema validation fails twice, what's recorded and what's returned to the caller?
[06:58] Maya: Flow: model output -> schema validation. If mismatch, Redwood can run auto-corrections (sanitizer), then retry. If still failing, we return an explicit error object indicating validation failure and include the last raw output and schema diff in the response if configured. You can also configure to route to a human-in-loop queue.
[07:20] Jon: Our platform team will want a sample payload to vet the schema enforcement. Can you drop a sample?
[07:26] Aaron: We'll include that in the follow-up email and the demo deck.
[07:30] (Maya runs another interactive demo showing a malformed output being auto-sanitized)
[08:05] Maya: Notice here - model initially returned risk_score as string "low" instead of integer 23. The sanitizer maps some heuristics and retries with a system prompt forcing numeric output; if that fails, we send back a structured error.
[08:20] Sana: How does Redwood prevent hallucinated merchant identifiers? If model invents merchant IDs, that causes bad writes.
[08:28] Maya: We recommend combining schema enforcement with allowlist checks and verification via tool calls. For critical writes, Redwood supports double-check: the model proposes a tool call payload but the platform can validate the payload against your internal DB before executing destructive actions.
[08:44] Mark: Let's talk about costs. Our cost model expects per-transaction averaged token usage < 200 tokens. We're worried about retries and function calls inflating token counts.
[08:55] Aaron: That's common. Our Optimize tooling can recommend batching, caching prefixes, and quantized model profiles to reduce token usage. For function-calling, often the model emits a small tool call payload which is low token overhead, and the heavy work is offloaded to your tool endpoint (which you control).
[09:12] Jon: Batching - do you support micro-batching for short latency-sensitive requests? Some workloads benefit from continuous batching but we need latency guarantees.
[09:20] Maya: Continuous batching has tunable thresholds - max_wait_ms and max_batch_size. For strict latency, set max_wait_ms low or use Dedicated with lower contention.
[09:30] (short pause)
[09:33] Maya: Now I want to demo a tool calling chain: model suggests merchant_enrich, then we call a fraud scoring microservice, and finally write an enrichment record. I'll simulate failures to show fallback.
[09:50] (demo)
[10:05] Maya: You can see the event trace: request -> model -> tool_call merchant_enrich -> tool returns mcc -> model then calls fraud_score -> returns risk_score -> Redwood returns final structured JSON. Each hop has a trace id and timing.
[10:20] Mark: Exporting traces - can those ship to our tracing backend?
[10:25] Maya: Yes, OTel-compatible traces can be forwarded to your collector.
[10:30] Jon: On schema enforcement - is there a DSL for corrections or only retries? e.g., if a string should be integer, can you coerce?
[10:38] Maya: There are sanitizer rules you can configure: coercion rules, allowlists, and regex validation. Those run before retrying.
[10:45] Sana: For model updates, can you run a validation harness against a held-out prompt set?
[10:50] Maya: Redwood Optimize provides evals and regression alerts. You can provide prompt sets and expected schema; we run nightly checks and alert on regressions.
[11:00] (Mark briefly steps away)
[11:15] Maya: Quick note: we sometimes see transcription glitches in the console; forgive the labeling - it's showing "Redwood In force" in the transcript sometimes.
[11:22] Mark (laugh): Yeah I thought that was a new product.
[11:28] Maya: (laughs) No, just our speech-to-text.
[11:33] Aaron: Back to security - we heard PCI and SOC 2 are big asks. Our security package includes SOC 2 reports, SAML/SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and support for KMS. For PCI, Private or Dedicated deployments with VPC peering are the typical route.
[11:50] Mark: How long does a Dedicated onboarding usually take? We want to pilot within 4 weeks if possible.
[11:57] Aaron: For a small pilot, 2-4 weeks is typical if we have clear access and test endpoints. Dedicated full production can take longer depending on contract and capacity scheduling.
[12:08] Sana: POC scope - we want to run 100k transactions over a week and measure latency and enrichment accuracy. Is that something Redwood will help benchmark?
[12:17] Maya: Yes, we do benchmark support. We'll run a joint benchmark using your sample traces and our Dedicated dev pool, capturing latency, token usage, and success rate for schema validation.
[12:28] Jon: What's included in the benchmark? We want to see p50/p95/p99, token distribution, and failure breakdowns.
[12:35] Maya: We'll provide a benchmark spreadsheet: per-route latency, token counts, retry counts, and resource utilization. We'll also include recommended model and quantization settings.
[12:45] Mark: Any competitors we should be aware of? We were also talking to OpenAI and Anthropic about function calling and to some infra vendors for self-hosted runtimes.
[12:55] Aaron: We compete largely with managed API providers in terms of ergonomics and with inference infra vendors on private deployments. Our differentiator is unified runtime and tooling for production economics: sampling, caching, retrys, and rollout controls.
[13:08] Sana: Can we get a write-up on your guardrail best practices for high-assurance outputs?
[13:14] Aaron: We'll include that in the follow-up.
[13:18] (Maya shows the API sample code - Node and Python snippets)
[13:30] Maya: Code sample: pass schema in the request, define the function signature, and set call_mode: "sync". On success you'll get back result.json and metadata.
[13:44] Jon: For the sync mode, what's the timeout default?
[13:48] Maya: Default is 60s but you can set per-route timeouts; for payment flows you'll likely set 2s-3s depending on service SLAs.
[14:00] Mark: If the function call to our enrichment service times out, do you return a partial result?
[14:06] Maya: Options: return structured error, return best-effort partial response, or fall back to cached enrichment. You configure fallback policies per route.
[14:18] Sana: We need a policy that never writes bad data - prefer human review over silent fallback.
[14:24] Aaron: That can be codified - Redwood supports per-route policies to require manual approval for certain failure classes.
[14:33] (brief silence)
[14:36] Maya: I'm going to run a stress demo now - firing a batch of 200 short requests to show batching and cache hits. Results are streaming in the console.
[14:50] (demo)
[15:05] Maya: You can see cache hits for repeated prefixes - significant token savings. The dashboard shows token breakdown and per-request latency.
[15:18] Jon: That dashboard is useful. Can we export token-level billing data to our billing system?
[15:24] Aaron: Yes, you can export CSVs or integrate via our cost APIs. For Dedicated we can provide detailed token-level reporting as part of the commitment.
[15:35] Mark: Any gotchas with embeddings or reranking for downstream enrichment? We're mostly doing structured output not embeddings but might add similarity checks later.
[15:44] Maya: Embeddings are a separate API but you can combine them; Redwood supports hybrid pipelines. Just be mindful of cross-model orchestration and cost.
[15:55] Sana: Can you show the rollout UI for pinning model versions?
[15:58] Maya: Sure - here's the route config. You can pin, enable canary (percent traffic), set fallback models, and add quality gates.
[16:08] Mark: For canaries, can we route based on request attributes (e.g., only internal traffic)?
[16:13] Maya: Yes, routing policies support attributes like customer_id, header values, or geo.
[16:18] Jon: Ok what's the proposed POC next steps?
[16:22] Aaron: Proposed: 1) Share security docs and pilot contract 2) Provide demo artifacts and sample schemas 3) Run a 2-week benchmark with 100k transactions on Dedicated dev pool 4) Check-in after benchmark to decide Dedicated vs Private.
[16:34] Mark: Sounds good. We'll need pricing for the pilot and projected cost for production.
[16:39] Aaron: We'll include a pricing sheet and a sample estimate for your QPS and token profile.
[16:44] (Silence while Aaron types notes)
[16:50] Maya: Any other technical questions?
[16:53] Sana: One more: do you support fine-grained RBAC for routes? Only a subset of engineers should be able to change route configs.
[16:59] Maya: Yes - SSO + RBAC with roles and granular permissions on routes, models, and audit views.
[17:06] Mark: Great. I'm going to loop in our security lead.
[17:10] Jon: We'll also share a sample of our transaction logs for the benchmark.
[17:14] Aaron: Excellent. We'll follow up with everything.
[17:18] (wrap)
[17:25] Aaron: Quick recap: We'll send security pack, sample schema and API snippets, benchmark plan and pricing. Maya will own the benchmark run and SE support.
[17:36] Maya: I'll send the deck and the sample payloads by Friday.
[17:40] Mark: Thanks everyone. That was helpful.
[17:44] Aaron: Thanks all - we'll follow up with next steps.

End of transcript. Some speech-to-text glitchiness present (names mis-typed in console).
